name: Reading the Results Honestly
title: Reading the Results Honestly
answer: Reading the results honestly means treating a pilot's numbers as a claim to be tested, not a verdict to be announced. It matters because volunteer teachers, novelty, weak comparison points, and average scores can all make a tool look better than it is. The idea asks schools to separate the tool's effect from these other forces before deciding to scale.

sections.body: When a pilot ends, the district needs to read the numbers carefully. Pilot teachers are often volunteers who like technology, and they may be strong teachers, so their classrooms could do better with any new tool. A comparison group of similar classrooms is therefore essential, because without it the district cannot tell the tool's effect from the teacher's. The idea also warns that novelty can make students work harder at first, and that a promising result should be checked again later in the year. It solves the problem of scaling a tool on a misleading early signal.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school sets up the pilot with similar classrooms as a comparison group, then reads results against that group rather than against no tool at all. The fair comparison is the new tool against the best current option, not an empty classroom. A promising early result is checked again later in the year, because a six week pilot can catch a novelty bump and mistake it for a lasting gain. The school also reports results separately for students with disabilities, English learners, and students from low income families whenever the numbers are large enough to mean something. The text does not give grade band examples, so the same steps apply across grades.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, and it supports the idea with two reviews. It cites a review of generative AI studies (Liu et al., 2025) with the finding that the boost to student motivation shrank the longer a study ran. It also cites one review (Letourneau, 2025) with the finding that intelligent tutoring systems helped students in general, but that the advantage shrank when they were compared with other practice software rather than with no software at all. These are the book's stated evidence for reading pilot results with caution.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that a pilot can mislead if it is read too quickly or too narrowly. Volunteer teachers may be unusually strong, novelty may fade, and a tool that beats nothing may not beat what the school already has. An average gain can hide a split where some students improved and others fell behind, so results for students with disabilities, English learners, and students from low income families should be reported separately whenever the numbers are large enough to mean something. A tool that widens a gap should not scale, even if the average looks good. The decision to scale stays with people, who must weigh the comparison group, the later check, and the subgroup results rather than letting a single average decide.
